title: How to Infuse Tea, Coffee and Herbs into Cupcakes
summaryShort: To infuse flavor into cupcakes, steep tea, coffee or herbs in warm milk, cream or melted butter for 10 to 20 minutes. Strain well, measure the liquid again, and use it in place of the plain dairy in your recipe.
metaTitle: How to Infuse Tea, Coffee and Herbs into Cupcakes
metaDescription: Learn how to infuse flavor into cupcakes with tea, coffee and herbs. Get steeping ratios, times and tips to avoid bitterness. Start baking today!
sidebarBullets: Tea: 2 tbsp loose leaf per 1 cup milk, steep 10 minutes.
Coffee: 1/4 cup coarse grounds per 1 cup milk, steep 10 minutes
Soft herbs: 1 packed cup per 1 cup cream, steep 20 minutes.
Heat dairy to steaming, never boiling.
Strain, then top up to the original measure.

sections.heading: What infusing does that extracts and powders can't
paragraphs: Infusing pulls aroma and gentle flavor out of an ingredient and into fat or dairy, so the taste feels baked in rather than added on top. Extracts are loud and simple, while an infusion tastes rounder and more like the real thing.
Milk, cream and butter all carry flavor well because aroma compounds dissolve in fat and cling to milk proteins. That is why a cup of Earl Grey milk tastes like Earl Grey, not just tea water.
In my kitchen, infused dairy gives the most natural result for tea, coffee and delicate herbs. For a quick boost, an extract still works, and I cover that in the extracts guide linked at the end.

sections.heading: Steeping in milk or cream: ratios and times
paragraphs: Heat 1 cup of milk or cream until it steams, about 180°F, then add your flavor and steep for 10 to 20 minutes. Boiling dairy scorches and pulls out harsh flavors, so keep the heat gentle.
Cover the pot while it steeps so the aroma stays in the liquid. Taste at the 10 minute mark, because you can always steep longer but you can't undo a bitter infusion.
Use these starting ratios per 1 cup of dairy:.
list: Black or Earl Grey tea: 2 tbsp loose leaf (or 3 tea bags), 10 minutes.
Chai or spiced tea: 2 tbsp loose leaf, 12 to 15 minutes.
Coffee: 1/4 cup coarse grounds or 1/2 cup whole beans, 10 minutes
Fresh mint or basil: 1 packed cup of leaves, 20 minutes.

sections.heading: Infusing butter for a richer flavor
paragraphs: Infuse butter by melting it on low heat with your tea or herbs, then letting it sit off the heat for 15 minutes. Butter holds flavor longer than milk, so it suits herbs like rosemary, thyme and lavender.
Use 1/4 cup of loose tea or 2 sprigs of woody herbs per 1 cup of butter. Keep the heat low so the milk solids don't brown, unless you want that nutty taste from the brown butter guide.
Strain through a fine sieve, then chill until the butter is soft but firm again. Expect to lose a few tablespoons to the leaves, so start with a little extra and weigh what you need.

sections.heading: Straining and measuring so your batter stays balanced
paragraphs: Strain the infusion through a fine mesh sieve, press gently, then add plain dairy until you are back to the original amount. Leaves and grounds soak up 15 to 20 percent of the liquid, and a short measure makes dense cupcakes.
Don't squeeze tea bags hard or mash the leaves. Pressing releases tannins, the compounds that make tea taste dry and bitter.
Cool the strained liquid before it meets your eggs or butter. Warm milk can curdle eggs and melt creamed butter, which ruins the crumb.

sections.heading: Keeping bitterness out
paragraphs: Bitterness comes from steeping too long, using water or dairy that is too hot, or squeezing the leaves. Stick to the times above and the flavor stays smooth.
Coffee turns harsh after about 10 minutes in hot milk. For a mellow taste, try a cold steep instead: stir 1/4 cup coarse grounds into 1 cup cold milk and chill overnight.
list: Use coarse grounds and whole leaves, not fine dust.
Taste before you strain, and stop when it is strong enough.
Add a pinch of salt to the batter to round out sharp edges.
Skip flavored teas with oils you don't recognize.

sections.heading: When to use matcha or instant espresso instead
paragraphs: Use a powder when you want strong color or deep flavor without extra liquid. Matcha and instant espresso dissolve right into the batter, so there is nothing to strain.

Whisk 1 to 2 tbsp matcha into the dry ingredients and remove 2 tbsp of flour to keep the balance. For coffee, dissolve 1 to 2 tbsp instant espresso in 1 tbsp hot water before adding it to the wet mix.
Powders also work in frosting, where a hot infusion would thin the buttercream. Sift them first so you don't get green or brown specks.

howToSteps: Choose your flavor and measure it using the ratio table.
Heat 1 cup of milk or cream until it steams, about 180°F.
Add the tea, coffee or herbs, cover, and steep 10 to 20 minutes.
Taste at 10 minutes and stop when the flavor is strong enough.
Strain through a fine sieve without pressing hard.
Add plain dairy to get back to the original measure.
Cool the liquid completely before adding it to the batter.
Use it in place of the milk or cream in your cupcake recipe.

faq.question: Can I use tea bags instead of loose leaf tea?
faq.answer: Yes. Use about 3 tea bags per 1 cup of milk and steep for 10 minutes. Lift them out without squeezing so the tea stays smooth.

faq.question: Why does my infused milk taste weak in the baked cupcake?
faq.answer: Baking mutes delicate flavors, so make the infusion stronger than you would drink it. Add an extra tablespoon of tea or steep 3 to 5 minutes longer, but keep tasting.

faq.question: Can I infuse plant milk the same way?
faq.answer: Yes, oat and soy milk steep well at the same temperature and time. Thin almond milk can taste watery, so use a little extra flavor.

faq.question: How far ahead can I make infused milk or butter?
faq.answer: Infused milk keeps in the fridge for up to 3 days. Infused butter keeps for up to a week, and both should be brought to room temperature before baking.

faq.question: Can I use fresh herbs and dried herbs the same way?
faq.answer: Use about one third as much dried herb as fresh. Dried lavender, for example, is strong, so 1 tbsp per cup is plenty.
